questions.question: The four-part specificity tuple (a,b,c,d) maps to:
questions.explanation: Standard order: inline styles, then IDs, then classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, then elements/pseudo-elements.

questions.question: An attribute selector [type='text'] has specificity equal to:
questions.explanation: Attributes and pseudo-classes sit in the class tier (0,0,1,0) — higher than elements but below IDs.

questions.question: Two competing rules, one .a.b (0,0,2,0) and one #c .d (0,1,1,0): which wins?

options.text: #c .d (it has an ID, so it wins regardless of class count)

questions.explanation: IDs outrank all classes. Compare left-to-right; the ID tier decides before class count matters.

questions.question: Inline style + !important vs a stylesheet !important: which wins?

options.text: The inline !important wins over a non-inline !important

questions.explanation: Among !important declarations, inline !important beats author !important (a known quirk). Avoid !important to stay sane.

questions.question: To override a third-party rule without !important, you can:

options.text: Increase specificity (add a class/element or use a more specific selector)

questions.explanation: Raising specificity beats the other rule cleanly. BEM-style double-class selectors (.comp .comp-part) are a common tactic.

questions.question: Why is '!important' considered a code smell?

options.text: It breaks the normal cascade, is hard to override, and signals specificity problems

questions.explanation: Overusing !important hides root causes (poor specificity) and creates escalating overrides. Reserve for rare edge cases.

questions.question: The universal selector * and pseudo-class :where() both contribute:
questions.explanation: * and :where() add no specificity, making them safe for resets and easy overrides (unlike :is which adopts inner specificity).

questions.question: Specificity is calculated PER DECLARATION'S SELECTOR, meaning:

options.text: Each selector's specificity is compared independently, not summed across a rule
All selectors on an element are summed

questions.explanation: The winning value comes from the most specific selector that sets that property — selectors for other properties don't add in.
